title: Karna's abandonment
hook: a girl in a king's house is given a mantra by a sage, and tries it on the sun
carry: I only wanted to see if it worked

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the birth of the cousins: rough play, a poisoned meal, and a grudge that started young. Did any small resentment show up, and did you name it? Day seven hundred twenty-eight.

Two days ago, Kunti told Pandu about a sage's mantra, and held one piece back. Today the poem steps back in time and tells that piece. Before Kunti was a queen, she was a girl called Pritha, raised in the house of a king named Kuntibhoja. When the sage Durvasa came as a guest, the hard work of looking after him fell to her, and she did it well. His gift was the mantra. And now she is young, unmarried, alone with words that can summon a god. Today Karna's abandonment begins, with a girl wondering whether the words really work.
screen: `PRITHA, IN KUNTIBHOJA'S HOUSE.` → `DURVASA'S GIFT.` → `DO THE WORDS WORK?`

segments.voice: With Durvasa's mantra, he told her, she could call any god she liked, and that god would come to her and give her a son. Then he left. And the text says that, out of curiosity, she tries it. She looks up at the sun rising, and she speaks the mantra. And Surya, the sun god, comes. Here the story slows down, because Pritha is frightened. She tells him she only wanted to see if the gift worked. She's a girl in her father's house. She asks him to go. And Surya answers that a god called by this mantra can't return for nothing. A son will be born. But he promises her something too: that she'll remain a maiden afterward, her honor kept. So on the week's last day, the story hands us a new beginning, older than all the others. Before the five brothers, before the cousins, Kunti had a son. Nobody in the palace knows it. Notice how human the scene is. There's no villain in it. There's a sage's gift, a girl's curiosity, a god who keeps the rules of the mantra, and fear. And out of that fear, over the next few days, will come a choice that echoes through the whole poem.
screen: `A SAGE'S GIFT: A MANTRA.` · `SHE TRIES IT ON THE SUN.` · `SURYA COMES, AND SHE IS AFRAID.` · `A SON BEFORE ALL THE OTHERS.` · then, large: `NOBODY IN THE PALACE KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, and a week to look back on. Let the breath slow down. Bring to mind one thing you started this week, maybe a little out of curiosity, the way Pritha tried those words. A conversation, a habit, a question. Don't decide yet whether it was wise. Just look at it, and see where it might lead. If you'd like, rest your attention on the morning light, wherever it fell for you today. The bell holds the time.
Karna's abandonment. It begins here: a mantra from Durvasa, a girl's curiosity, and the sun answering her call.
Your line: I only wanted to see if it worked. Today, before you try something just to see what happens, pause one breath and ask where it leads. Day seven hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Some Hindus greet the rising sun with folded hands or an offering of water, honoring Surya, the god Pritha called with Durvasa's mantra.

fork.setup: you're Pritha. a sage has given you words that can call any god. you're young and alone with them. what do you do?
options: put the words away and never use them.
try them once, on the rising sun, to see if they work.
tell your father and ask what to do.
fork.reveal: out of curiosity, she tries them on the sun. Surya comes, and a son is promised before anyone in the palace knows.

original.note: Sanskrit sūrya: the sun, and the sun god who answers Pritha's mantra.

trapdoor: what you thought: Karna's story starts with a baby in a basket.
what it means: it starts earlier, with a girl, a sage's mantra and her curiosity about the rising sun.
what a scholar hears: Kunti's son by Surya is born before her marriage, so Karna is older than all five brothers, a fact the story keeps hidden for a long time.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Sambhava Parva (Pritha in Kuntibhoja's house; Durvasa's mantra; Pritha summons Surya)
